# Error index

<!-- Generated by tools/gen-error-index.py. Edit crates/evocc/explain/*.md. -->

Each example is checked by the explanation-page tests.
A runtime example describes an executed path, not all possible inputs.
`Trigger: none` states why a code has no C trigger in this profile.

## E0xxx

### E0102: unmatched-conditional

A conditional directive has no matching opening or closing directive.
The preprocessor cannot determine which source belongs to the conditional.

Each `#if`, `#ifdef` and `#ifndef` needs one matching `#endif`.
An `#else` or `#elif` must belong to an open conditional.

```c
#endif
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
#if 1
int main(void) { return 0; }
#endif
```

### E0104: error-directive

The preprocessor reached an active `#error` directive.
The text after the directive describes the source author's requirement.

This directive deliberately stops translation when a source condition is not met.
Correct the configuration instead of removing a required check.

```c
#ifndef BUFFER_SIZE
#error define BUFFER_SIZE before this point
#endif
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
#define BUFFER_SIZE 64
#ifndef BUFFER_SIZE
#error define BUFFER_SIZE before this point
#endif
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

### E0105: include-not-found

The preprocessor cannot find the requested header.
The include search paths do not contain a readable matching file.

A source file cannot use declarations from a header that was not read.
Install the header or correct its name and include path.

```c
#include "evocc-example-missing-header.h"
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

For this self-contained program, no header is needed.

```c
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

### E0106: feature-query-malformed

A feature query has invalid arguments or missing punctuation.
The preprocessor cannot evaluate the query.

Each query has a specific argument form.
For example, `__has_attribute` takes one attribute name in parentheses.

```c
#if __has_attribute()
#endif
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
#if __has_attribute(unused)
#define UNUSED __attribute__((unused))
#else
#define UNUSED
#endif
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

### E0107: pragma-pack-unsupported

A `#pragma pack` request is malformed or outside the supported forms.
EvoCC refuses to guess the record layout.

Packing changes member offsets and object alignment.
Use a supported packing request and restore it after the affected declarations.

```c
#pragma pack(show)
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
#pragma pack(push, 1)
struct Packet { char tag; int value; };
#pragma pack(pop)
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

### E0108: poisoned-identifier-used

The preprocessor found a use of an identifier marked with `#pragma GCC poison`.
That directive forbids later direct uses of the name.

Headers can use poisoning to reject an obsolete interface.
Replace the forbidden name with the permitted interface.

```c
#pragma GCC poison obsolete
int main(void) { int obsolete = 0; return obsolete; }
```

```c
#pragma GCC poison obsolete
int main(void) { int current = 0; return current; }
```

### E0109: counter-overflow

The diagnostic contract assigns this code to exhaustion of `__COUNTER__`.
The specified limit is 2^32 expansions in one translation unit.

Reusing counter values can break generated names that must be distinct.
This is an EvoCC extension limit, not an ISO C integer expression rule.

Trigger: none
Reason: the current preprocessor wraps its u32 counter and does not emit this code.

This is a known difference between the implementation and the diagnostic contract.
There is no tested C trigger or compiler-side fix in this explanation package.
Reduce generated expansions or split the translation unit before that limit.

### E0110: invalid-token-paste

A macro `##` operation does not produce one preprocessing token.
The preprocessor cannot use the combined spelling as a token.

Token pasting joins spellings, not C expressions.
Use separate tokens for an arithmetic operation.

```c
#define JOIN(a, b) a ## b
int main(void) { return JOIN(1, +); }
```

```c
#define SUM(a, b) ((a) + (b))
int main(void) { return SUM(1, 2); }
```

### E0111: conditional-operand-not-integer

A preprocessor conditional contains a number that is not an integer constant.
The preprocessor cannot evaluate it as a conditional operand.

The expression in `#if` uses integer preprocessing arithmetic.
Use an integer condition instead of a floating constant.

```c
#if 1.5
#endif
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
#if 1
#endif
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

### E0112: stray-token

The source contains a token that cannot be used at this point.
Macro expansion can also produce such a token.

Every remaining preprocessing token must have a valid C token form.
Remove the stray character or correct the macro that produced it.

```c
int main(void) { return @; }
```

```c
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

### E0113: directive-in-macro-argument

An unsupported directive appears while a macro argument is being collected.
EvoCC refuses to expand that argument with an unspecified directive effect.

The GNU-compatible argument collector permits only its documented directive forms.
Move a pragma outside the macro invocation so its position is explicit.

```c
#define ID(x) x
ID(int value;
#pragma GCC diagnostic push
)
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
#define ID(x) x
#pragma GCC diagnostic push
ID(int value;)
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

## E1xxx

### E1003: expected-expression

The parser needs an expression at this position.
An operator or delimiter cannot supply the missing value by itself.

C expressions must have the operands required by their operators.
Add the operand, or remove an operator that you did not intend to use.

```c
int main(void) { return !; }
```

```c
int main(void) { return !1; }
```

### E1005: invalid-declarator

This declaration combines type constructors in an invalid order.
For example, it can declare an array of functions instead of function pointers.

C permits arrays of objects, but a function is not an object.
Declare pointers when an array must refer to functions.

```c
int handlers[2](int argument);
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
int (*handlers[2])(int argument);
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

### E1207: invalid-return-value

The return statement does not match the function's result type.
It can supply a value to a void function or omit a required value.

C uses the declared result type to check each return statement.
Return a value of the required type, or declare a void function when appropriate.

```c
void stop(void) { return 1; }
int main(void) { stop(); return 0; }
```

```c
void stop(void) { return; }
int main(void) { stop(); return 0; }
```

### E1306: enumerator-outside-underlying-type

An enumerator value does not fit the fixed underlying type of its enumeration.
An enumeration written `enum E : T` has the range of `T`.
Each value, written or the previous value plus one, must be representable in `T`.
C23 makes this a constraint violation, and GCC 14 rejects it in every language mode.
Choose a wider underlying type, or change the value.

```c
enum level : unsigned char { low = 1, high = 256 };
int main(void) { return low - 1; }
```

```c
enum level : unsigned short { low = 1, high = 256 };
int main(void) { return low - 1; }
```

### E1307: invalid-enumeration-underlying-type

The fixed underlying type of an enumeration is not valid here.
The type after the colon in `enum E : T` must be an integer type, such as `unsigned char`.
Without an enumerator list, `enum E : T` may only form the declaration `enum E : T;`.
Every declaration of the enumeration must name the same type, and its definition too.

```c
enum mode : int;
enum mode { off, on };
int main(void) { return off; }
```

```c
enum mode : int;
enum mode : int { off, on };
int main(void) { return off; }
```

## E2xxx

### E2001: undeclared-identifier

The name has no declaration visible at this use.
A declaration in another scope does not make the name visible here.

C resolves an identifier using its scope and declaration.
Declare the object or function before use, and check the spelling of its name.

```c
int main(void) { return count; }
```

```c
int main(void) { int count = 0; return count; }
```

### E2002: incompatible-redeclaration

Two declarations of one name do not describe compatible entities.
The conflict can involve its type, linkage, or definition.

C requires declarations that refer to the same entity to agree.
Correct the conflicting declaration instead of casting each use.

```c
int count;
double count;
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
extern int count;
int count = 0;
int main(void) { return count; }
```

### E2202: invalid-initializer-type

The supplied value cannot initialize or convert to the required type.
This code also covers incompatible assignment and return conversions.

C constrains conversions between scalar, pointer, and aggregate types.
Use a compatible value rather than a cast that hides the type error.

```c
int *value = 1.5;
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
int object = 0;
int *value = &object;
int main(void) { return *value; }
```

### E2203: variable-length-object

A variable-length object occurs in a context that EvoCC refuses.
One such context is an initializer for a variable-length array.

In the supported C11 profile, a variable-length array cannot have an initializer.
Create the array first and assign its elements during execution.

```c
int main(void) { int n = 2; int a[n] = {1}; return 0; }
```

```c
int main(void) {
    int n = 2;
    int a[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) a[i] = 0;
    return a[0];
}
```

### E2208: non-constant-static-initializer

A static-storage initializer requires a value that is not constant at translation.
Calling a function in that initializer is one example.

C requires static-storage initialization to use permitted constant expressions.
Move the computation into a function that runs before the value is used.

```c
int initial(void) { return 0; }
static int value = initial();
int main(void) { return value; }
```

```c
int initial(void) { return 0; }
static int value;
int main(void) { value = initial(); return value; }
```

### E2702: atomic-update-unsupported

This access of an atomic object is outside EvoCC's supported atomic operations.
A floating compound assignment to an atomic object is one such access.

EvoCC admits loads, stores and integer or pointer updates of 1-, 2-, 4- and 8-byte atomic scalars.
A floating update, a whole-record access and a 16-byte atomic object stay refused.

```c
static _Atomic double value = 3;
int main(void) { value += 4; return 0; }
```

Fix: none

Keep the atomic requirement and use a compiler that supports this operation.
Removing `_Atomic` is safe only when the program does not require atomic access.

### E2902: not-covered: compound-literal

This withdrawn code identified unsupported compound literals.
Current EvoCC lowers compound literals and must not reuse this code.

A compound literal creates an unnamed object with an initializer.
The implementation now tracks that object's storage and lifetime.

Trigger: none
Reason: the diagnostic authority table marks this code as withdrawn.

```c
struct Pair { int x, y; };
int main(void) {
    struct Pair pair = (struct Pair){0, 1};
    return pair.x;
}
```

### E2903: malformed-attribute

An attribute has invalid syntax or an invalid argument.
The diagnostic identifies the attribute EvoCC could not apply.

Attributes can change layout, linkage, or generated code.
EvoCC rejects malformed attributes instead of silently applying another meaning.

```c
typedef int Aligned __attribute__((aligned(3)));
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
typedef int Aligned __attribute__((aligned(8)));
int main(void) { Aligned value = 0; return value; }
```

### E2904: not-covered: variably-modified-typeof

This `typeof` type name needs a runtime bound outside a function body.
EvoCC cannot capture that bound in the declared scope.

A GNU `typeof` operand of variably modified type requires evaluation.
Put the variable-length type in a function body, where the bound can execute.

```c
int n = 2;
typeof(int[n]) *p;
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
int main(void) {
    int n = 2;
    typeof(int[n]) a;
    return sizeof a != 2 * sizeof(int);
}
```

### E2905: statement-expression-outside-function

A GNU statement expression appears outside a function body.
The `({ ... })` form is not permitted at this position.

Statement expressions provide executable statements inside expressions.
Use a constant initializer at file scope, or move the statements into a function.

```c
int value = ({ 0; });
int main(void) { return value; }
```

```c
int value = 0;
int main(void) { return value; }
```

### E2906: designator-outside-object

A member or element designator does not select part of the specified object.
This also applies to a member path in `__builtin_offsetof`.

C layout queries and designated initializers need a valid subobject.
Use a member or index that exists in the declared type.

```c
struct Item { int value; };
unsigned long offset = __builtin_offsetof(struct Item, missing);
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
struct Item { int value; };
unsigned long offset = __builtin_offsetof(struct Item, value);
int main(void) { return offset != 0; }
```

### E2907: generic-selection-duplicate-association

A `_Generic` selection has two associations with compatible types.
More than one `default` association also causes this diagnostic.

C requires a generic selection to identify at most one matching association.
Remove the duplicate and keep one result for each compatible type.

```c
int main(void) { return _Generic(0, int: 0, int: 1); }
```

```c
int main(void) { return _Generic(0, int: 0, default: 1); }
```

### E2908: generic-selection-no-match

No association matches the controlling type of `_Generic`.
The selection also has no `default` association.

C requires a generic selection to produce exactly one selected expression.
Add the needed type association or a suitable default result.

```c
int main(void) { return _Generic(0, double: 1); }
```

```c
int main(void) { return _Generic(0, double: 1, int: 0); }
```

### E2909: builtin-arity

A builtin has the wrong number of operands.
Each recognized builtin has a fixed operand contract.

EvoCC needs every required operand to apply the builtin's semantics.
Use the documented operand count instead of relying on ordinary variadic calls.

```c
int main(void) { return __builtin_expect(0); }
```

```c
int main(void) { return __builtin_expect(0, 0); }
```

### E2910: builtin-not-called

A special builtin appears as a value rather than a builtin invocation.
This builtin does not have an ordinary function address.

Some builtins are compiler syntax with operand-specific rules.
Invoke the builtin directly instead of storing its name as a value.

```c
int main(void) { return __builtin_constant_p; }
```

```c
int main(void) { return !__builtin_constant_p(1); }
```

### E2911: static-assertion-failed

A `_Static_assert` condition evaluated to zero.
The message supplied by the source describes the condition that must hold.

C checks static assertions during translation, not during program execution.
Correct the violated requirement and keep a useful assertion for that requirement.

```c
_Static_assert(sizeof(char) == 2, "one byte required");
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
_Static_assert(sizeof(char) == 1, "one byte required");
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

### E2912: static-assertion-not-constant

A required integer constant expression could not be evaluated as one.
Static assertions and some builtin operands require this form.

These checks need a translation-time value, not a value read during execution.
Use an integer constant expression or move a runtime check into executable code.

```c
int limit = 4;
_Static_assert(limit > 0, "positive limit required");
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
enum { limit = 4 };
_Static_assert(limit > 0, "positive limit required");
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

### E2913: builtin-operand-not-convertible

A builtin operand cannot meet the builtin's required type or value category.
The builtin cannot use that operand as an ordinary implicit conversion.

Builtins have specific contracts for pointers, storage, and scalar types.
Supply an operand of the required kind instead of hiding the mismatch with a cast.

```c
int main(void) { return __builtin_strlen(L"a") != 1; }
```

```c
int main(void) { return __builtin_strlen("a") != 1; }
```

### E2914: malformed-asm

An assembly declaration has invalid syntax or invalid operands.
For example, an output constraint can name an expression that is not writable.

The compiler must know where assembly reads and writes values.
Correct the operands and constraints before asking the backend to emit assembly.

```c
int main(void) { asm("" : "=r"(1)); return 0; }
```

```c
int main(void) { int value = 0; return value; }
```

The fixed example removes an unnecessary assembly statement.
The interpreter does not execute arbitrary machine assembly.

### E2915: auto-type-misuse

A GNU `__auto_type` declaration does not have a supported deduction form.
It needs one plain named object with an initializer.

The initializer supplies the type of the object.
Add an initializer or write the object's type explicitly.

```c
int main(void) { __auto_type value; return 0; }
```

```c
int main(void) { __auto_type value = 0; return value; }
```

### E2916: case-range-invalid

A switch case or GNU case range cannot form a valid set of case values.
The bounds must be constant and must not conflict with another case.

A switch must select an unambiguous destination for each matching value.
Correct the bounds and remove overlapping or duplicate cases.

```c
int main(void) {
    switch (2) { case 3 ... 1: return 1; default: return 0; }
}
```

```c
int main(void) {
    switch (2) { case 1 ... 3: return 0; default: return 1; }
}
```

### E2917: designator-index-not-constant

An array initializer designator does not give a valid constant index or range.
A runtime variable cannot specify that position.

C uses initializer designators to select subobjects during translation.
Use a nonnegative integer constant expression within the array's bounds.

```c
int main(void) { int i = 0; int a[2] = {[i] = 1}; return 0; }
```

```c
int main(void) { int a[2] = {[0] = 1}; return a[0] != 1; }
```

### E2918: jump-into-statement-expression

A jump enters a GNU statement expression from outside that expression.
This skips the normal entry and evaluation of the expression.

GNU statement expressions do not permit jumps into their bodies.
Use ordinary function-scope control flow instead of a label inside an expression.

```c
int main(void) {
    goto inside;
    ({ inside: 1; });
    return 0;
}
```

```c
int main(void) {
    goto inside;
inside:
    return 0;
}
```

### E2919: flexible-array-initializer-not-static

An initializer tries to provide flexible-array elements in an unsupported storage context.
EvoCC supports its flexible-array initialization extension only for static storage.

A flexible array member does not contribute ordinary elements to the struct's size.
Use a fixed-size array when an automatic object must contain initialized elements.

```c
struct Packet { int length; int data[]; };
int main(void) { struct Packet p = {1, {0}}; return 0; }
```

```c
struct Packet { int length; int data[1]; };
int main(void) { struct Packet p = {1, {0}}; return p.data[0]; }
```

### E2920: undeclared-label

A branch refers to a label that has no definition in the function.
A label in another function does not satisfy this reference.

C labels have function scope and must name destinations in that function.
Correct the label name or add the intended destination.

```c
int main(void) { goto done; }
```

```c
int main(void) { goto done; done: return 0; }
```

### E2922: volatile-aggregate-copy-unsupported

A volatile aggregate copy requires an access pattern EvoCC does not support.
Examples include oversized unions and records with bit-fields.

Volatile accesses have observable behavior that a byte copy can change.
EvoCC refuses the copy instead of inventing an access width or order.

```c
union U { int narrow; long wide[2]; };
void copy(volatile union U *to, volatile union U *from) { *to = *from; }
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

Fix: none

Specify the required hardware access operations before replacing this copy.
Removing `volatile` is not a general fix.

### E2923: invalid-array-bound

An array declaration has an invalid bound.
A negative constant bound cannot describe an array object.

C array bounds must satisfy the requirements for their declaration context.
Use a valid size and check runtime sizes before creating variable-length arrays.

```c
int values[-1];
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
int values[1];
int main(void) { return values[0]; }
```

### E2924: attribute-on-non-null-statement

A statement attribute appears before a statement that is not a null statement.
EvoCC requires this attribute form to end with a semicolon.

An attribute's placement determines which entity it affects.
Put the attribute on a permitted statement instead of treating it as a prefix.

```c
int main(void) { __attribute__((unused)) return 0; }
```

```c
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

The fixed example removes an attribute with no useful statement target.

### E2925: builtin-mode-out-of-range

A builtin mode operand is outside the supported range.
For `__builtin_object_size`, the mode must be an integer constant from 0 to 3.

The mode selects distinct rules for the object-size query.
Choose the mode that describes the required query rather than an arbitrary integer.

```c
int main(void) { char a[4]; return __builtin_object_size(a, 4) != 4; }
```

```c
int main(void) { char a[4]; return __builtin_object_size(a, 0) != 4; }
```

### E2926: va-start-outside-variadic-function

`__builtin_va_start` appears outside a variadic function.
There is no unnamed argument sequence for it to initialize.

A variadic argument cursor belongs to the current variadic invocation.
Use it only in a function whose declaration ends with `...`.

```c
int main(void) {
    __builtin_va_list ap;
    __builtin_va_start(ap, 0);
    return 0;
}
```

```c
int first(int count, ...) {
    __builtin_va_list ap;
    __builtin_va_start(ap, count);
    int value = __builtin_va_arg(ap, int);
    __builtin_va_end(ap);
    return value;
}
int main(void) { return first(1, 0); }
```

### E2927: builtin-library-declaration-incompatible

A library declaration conflicts with the interface required by a builtin.
EvoCC cannot bind the builtin to a function of that type.

Builtin expansion must preserve the library function's calling interface.
Use the correct declaration, normally from the library's header.

```c
int strlen(int);
unsigned long size(char *p) { return __builtin_strlen(p); }
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
unsigned long strlen(const char *);
int main(void) { return __builtin_strlen("a") != 1; }
```

### E2928: address-of-register-object

The address operator is applied to an object declared `register`.
The restriction applies even when the compiler stores the object in memory.

C forbids taking the address of a register-declared object.
Remove `register` when the program needs the object's address.

```c
int main(void) { register int value = 0; int *p = &value; return *p; }
```

```c
int main(void) { int value = 0; int *p = &value; return *p; }
```

### E2929: unpromoted-va-arg-type

`__builtin_va_arg` requests a type changed by default argument promotion.
For example, an anonymous `char` argument arrives as `int`, not `char`.

C promotes narrow integers and promotes `float` to `double` in variadic calls.
Read the promoted type, then convert the value if a narrower type is needed.

```c
int first(int n, ...) {
    __builtin_va_list ap;
    __builtin_va_start(ap, n);
    return __builtin_va_arg(ap, char);
}
int main(void) { return first(1, 0); }
```

```c
int first(int n, ...) {
    __builtin_va_list ap;
    __builtin_va_start(ap, n);
    int value = __builtin_va_arg(ap, int);
    __builtin_va_end(ap);
    return value;
}
int main(void) { return first(1, 0); }
```

### E2930: use-with-incomplete-enumeration

An expression requires an enumeration type that is still incomplete.
A forward declaration alone does not supply its completed type information.

EvoCC needs the completed type to validate values and function interfaces.
Define the enumeration before a use that needs that information.

```c
enum Result;
enum Result result(void);
int main(void) { return result(); }
```

```c
enum Result { OK = 0 };
enum Result result(void) { return OK; }
int main(void) { return result(); }
```

### E2931: unprototyped-call-mismatch

Calls through an unprototyped external declaration disagree with each other.
The mismatch can involve the promoted argument types or their number.

An empty parameter list does not make arbitrary argument combinations valid.
Provide a prototype and make the calls agree with the definition.

```c
int take();
int main(void) { take(1); return take(1L); }
```

```c
int take(long value);
int main(void) { return take(1); }
int take(long value) { return value != 1; }
```

### E2932: always-inline-cycle

Required inline expansion follows a cycle of calls.
Expanding that cycle cannot produce a finite function body.

The `always_inline` requirement cannot be satisfied by recursive expansion.
Remove the requirement or rewrite the recursion as bounded control flow.

```c
static __attribute__((always_inline)) int down(int n) {
    return n ? down(n - 1) : 0;
}
int main(void) { return down(3); }
```

```c
static int down(int n) { return n ? down(n - 1) : 0; }
int main(void) { return down(3); }
```

### E2933: unsupported-termination-builtin

EvoCC refuses this termination builtin in the selected front-end profile.
The refusal does not mean that ordinary return statements are unsupported.

Process termination has effects beyond returning from an ordinary function.
EvoCC does not substitute an incomplete execution model for those effects.

```c
int main(void) { __builtin_exit(0); }
```

```c
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

Returning from `main` suffices for this example.
It is not a replacement for terminating a process from an arbitrary function.

### E2934: function-specifier-on-non-function

A function specifier is attached to something other than a permitted function declaration.
For example, `_Noreturn` cannot describe an integer object.

Function specifiers describe function behavior, not object storage.
Remove the specifier from the object declaration.

```c
_Noreturn int value;
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
int value;
int main(void) { return value; }
```

### E2935: unsupported-library-builtin

This library builtin is outside the selected EvoCC front-end profile.
EvoCC does not silently replace it with an operation of different behavior.

Library calls can have output, error, and environment effects.
A replacement must preserve those effects, not just the return type.

```c
int main(void) { return __builtin_puts("hello"); }
```

Fix: none

Use the library's ordinary declared interface for native compilation.
That does not establish interpreter support for the external call.

### E2936: invalid-line-directive

A `#line` directive has an invalid line number or operand form.
EvoCC cannot use it to set the following source location.

Line directives control the locations reported for subsequent source text.
Supply a valid positive line number and an optional quoted filename.

```c
#line nope
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
#line 1 "example.c"
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

### E2937: invalid-call-target

The expression before a call's parentheses is not callable.
An integer object is not a function or a function pointer.

C function calls require a function designator or a pointer to a function.
Call the intended function instead of a variable with a similar name.

```c
int main(void) { int result = 0; return result(); }
```

```c
int result(void) { return 0; }
int main(void) { return result(); }
```

### E2938: invalid-alignment-specifier

An alignment specifier requests an invalid or disallowed alignment.
It can also try to weaken the natural alignment of an object.

C alignment requirements must remain valid for the declared type and context.
Use a supported alignment that is at least as strict as the natural alignment.

```c
_Alignas(3) int value;
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
_Alignas(8) int value;
int main(void) { return value; }
```

### E2939: unsupported-wide-bit-field-promotion

An expression requires a wide bit-field promotion outside EvoCC's agreed target profile.
The field width can produce a type distinct from ordinary integer ranks.

Reference compiler behavior for these extensions is not uniform.
Use an explicit ordinary integer conversion when that is the intended arithmetic type.

```c
struct S { unsigned long x : 40; };
int main(void) { struct S s = {0}; return s.x == -1; }
```

```c
struct S { unsigned long x : 40; };
int main(void) { struct S s = {0}; return (unsigned long)s.x == -1; }
```

### E2940: unsupported-scalar-storage-order

The source requests a scalar storage order that EvoCC does not implement.
This attribute can change the byte order of record members.

Ignoring it would change the program's object representation.
Use explicit byte encoding when a data format needs a particular byte order.

```c
struct __attribute__((scalar_storage_order("big-endian"))) S { unsigned x; };
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
int main(void) {
    unsigned x = 258;
    unsigned char bytes[2] = {(unsigned char)(x >> 8), (unsigned char)x};
    return bytes[0] != 1 || bytes[1] != 2;
}
```

The fixed example encodes a two-byte field explicitly; it does not recreate the struct ABI.

### E2941: unsupported-type-classification

`__builtin_classify_type` received a type outside EvoCC's agreed classification profile.
For example, `_Bool` does not have one agreed classification in the reference compilers.

This GNU builtin reports compiler-specific type categories.
Use a direct type selection when the program needs a portable type distinction.

```c
int main(void) { return __builtin_classify_type((_Bool)0); }
```

```c
int main(void) { return _Generic((_Bool)0, _Bool: 0, default: 1); }
```

### E2942: incompatible-union-cast

A GNU cast to a union has no compatible member for the operand.
The cast cannot select a valid union member to initialize.

This extension selects a member by type, not by a byte reinterpretation of arbitrary data.
Use a compatible member value or an explicit member initializer.

```c
union Number { int value; };
int main(void) { union Number n = (union Number)1.5; return 0; }
```

```c
union Number { int value; };
int main(void) { union Number n = {.value = 0}; return n.value; }
```

### E2943: invalid-or-conflicting-symbol-attribute

A symbol attribute or visibility directive has an invalid or conflicting setting.
EvoCC cannot apply it while preserving one consistent symbol contract.

Linkage and visibility affect how other translation units refer to a symbol.
Correct the conflicting settings or balance the visibility directive stack.

```c
#pragma GCC visibility pop
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
#pragma GCC visibility push(hidden)
int helper(void) { return 0; }
#pragma GCC visibility pop
int main(void) { return helper(); }
```

### E2944: ordinary-builtin-binding-conflict

An ordinary name used for builtin behavior also has a conflicting source binding.
A source definition or assembly name can prevent one unambiguous binding.

Builtin expansion must not silently replace a program-defined implementation.
Give an unrelated helper a distinct name and preserve the intended call target.

```c
void *alloca(unsigned long);
int main(void) { return alloca(1) == 0; }
void *alloca(unsigned long n) { return (void *)0; }
```

```c
void *empty_buffer(unsigned long n) { return (void *)0; }
int main(void) { return empty_buffer(1) != 0; }
```

### E2945: jump-into-variable-type-scope

A jump enters the scope of a variably modified declaration from outside it.
The jump would skip the declaration's required evaluation.

C forbids this entry into the scope of a variably modified identifier.
Enter the scope normally before reaching the label.

```c
int main(void) {
    int n = 2;
    goto inside;
    int values[n];
inside:
    return 0;
}
```

```c
int main(void) {
    int n = 2;
    int values[n];
    goto inside;
inside:
    return 0;
}
```

### E2946: builtin-local-binding-conflict

A builtin library operation conflicts with a same-named function or linked object.
EvoCC does not choose silently between a local body and the library operation,
or emit an object under the name of a called library function.

The two implementations can have different behavior even with compatible types.
Use a distinct name for the local helper and call it explicitly.
For an object collision, use a distinct object name. A block-local object does
not have this linked-name conflict.

```c
static int strcmp(const char *a, const char *b) { return 0; }
int main(void) {
    char a[] = "a", b[] = "b";
    return __builtin_strcmp(a, b);
}
```

```c
static int same_first(const char *a, const char *b) { return a[0] == b[0]; }
int main(void) {
    char a[] = "a", b[] = "b";
    return same_first(a, b);
}
```

### E2947: invalid-atomic-memory-order

An atomic builtin has an invalid memory-order operand.
An order can be valid for one operation but invalid for another.

For example, a load cannot provide release ordering.
Choose an order permitted by the operation and sufficient for the synchronization protocol.

```c
int main(void) { int value = 0; return __atomic_load_n(&value, 3); }
```

```c
int main(void) { int value = 0; return __atomic_load_n(&value, 2); }
```

The example changes release (3) to acquire (2).
The required order in a concurrent program depends on its communication protocol.

### E2948: integer-complex-division-oracle-conflict

This withdrawn code identified integer-complex division.
Current EvoCC divides integer-complex values and must not reuse this code.

Integer-complex division uses GCC's wide algorithm in the component type.
Each step keeps the ordinary division-by-zero and overflow checks.

Trigger: none
Reason: the diagnostic authority table marks this code as withdrawn.

```c
int main(void) {
    _Complex int a = 4, b = 2;
    _Complex int result = a / b;
    return __real__ result - 2;
}
```

### E2949: unknown-builtin

A call names a `__builtin_`, `__atomic_` or `__sync_` function that EvoCC does not implement.
On Darwin, whose `<stdatomic.h>` is Clang's, a `__c11_atomic_` name is such a builtin too.
An implicit declaration cannot supply a compiler builtin, with or without `-w`.

The diagnostic names the builtin where it is spelled.
When a macro supplies the name, the location is the macro use.
Test `__has_builtin` before you call a builtin that a compiler can lack.

```c
int main(void) { return __builtin_not_implemented(0); }
```

```c
#if __has_builtin(__builtin_not_implemented)
#define VALUE() __builtin_not_implemented(0)
#else
#define VALUE() 0
#endif
int main(void) { return VALUE(); }
```

### E2950: invalid-va-arg-pack

`__builtin_va_arg_pack ()` or `__builtin_va_arg_pack_len ()` has no arguments to forward.
They stand for the anonymous arguments of a variadic function at a substituted call.

The pack must be the last argument of a call to a variadic function.
An `always_inline` variadic function is substituted at each direct call, so its body can forward the pack.
A body that stays an ordinary function, for example for its address, cannot forward it.

```c
static int count(int n, ...) { return n; }
int forward(int n) { return count(n, __builtin_va_arg_pack()); }
int main(void) { return forward(0); }
```

```c
static int count(int n, ...) { return n; }
static inline __attribute__((always_inline)) int forward(int n, ...) {
    return count(n, __builtin_va_arg_pack()) + __builtin_va_arg_pack_len();
}
int main(void) { return forward(0); }
```

### E2951: builtin-argument-type

A floating comparison or classification builtin received an operand of the wrong type.
The comparison builtins need two real operands with a floating type after the usual arithmetic conversions.

`__builtin_isgreater` and its family compare floating values without signaling on a quiet NaN.
Classification builtins such as `__builtin_isnan` inspect a floating representation.
`__builtin_fpclassify` also needs five class arguments that are integer constant expressions.
Convert an integer operand to a floating type, or use an ordinary integer comparison.

```c
int main(void) { return __builtin_isgreater(1, 2); }
```

```c
int main(void) { return __builtin_isgreater(1.0, 2.0); }
```

### E2952: unsupported-function-attribute

EvoCC does not implement this execution rule or calling convention.
An ordinary function is not a safe replacement.
A prototype can carry the attribute: EvoCC records it on that function.
The error then marks each definition of that function and each use of its
name, such as a call or an address, in code that the unit keeps.
A type, a typedef, an object or a member with the attribute is an error too.
`-w` does not suppress it.

Three attributes keep ordinary uses. A callee marked `aarch64_vector_pcs`,
`preserve_all` or `preserve_most` preserves more registers than its caller
relies on, so a call of it is an ordinary call. `returns_twice` is never this
error on a function: EvoCC gives its calls the rule of GCC 14.

A naked assembly function must not get an ordinary compiler frame. Keep such
a function in a separate assembly file, or use ordinary C if no special
calling convention is required. Do not remove an ABI attribute from a function
that must match an external caller.

```c
__attribute__((naked)) int value(void) { __asm__("mov w0, #7\n\tret"); }
int main(void) { return value() != 7; }
```

```c
int value(void) { return 7; }
int main(void) { return value() != 7; }
```

### E2953: incompatible-record-cast

A cast to a struct type has an operand of a different type.
Matching fields do not make two distinct struct tags compatible.

Use the original struct type, or initialize the destination's fields explicitly.
A cast to the same struct type is allowed and does not change its value.

```c
struct A { int x; };
struct B { int x; };
int main(void) {
    struct A a = { 3 };
    struct B b = (struct B)a;
    return b.x - 3;
}
```

```c
struct A { int x; };
struct B { int x; };
int main(void) {
    struct A a = { 3 };
    struct B b = { a.x };
    return b.x - 3;
}
```

### E2954: constant-string-binding-conflict

A later declaration changes an object used by a constant string query.
A weak, alias or assembly-name declaration can replace that
object, so its earlier initializer cannot remain the source of a constant.

Keep the binding fixed. If replacement is needed, declare the binding before
use and use an ordinary runtime call instead of an integer constant expression.

```c
const char text[] = "abc";
enum { length = __builtin_strlen(text) };
extern const char text[] __attribute__((weak));
int main(void) { return length - 3; }
```

```c
const char text[] = "abc";
enum { length = __builtin_strlen(text) };
int main(void) { return length - 3; }
```

### E2955: invalid-atomic-type

`_Atomic` names a type that cannot be atomic.
C11 forbids `_Atomic ( type-name )` for an array, function, atomic or qualified type.

The `_Atomic` qualifier also cannot apply to an array or function type.
EvoCC does not permit an atomic bit-field, as GCC and Clang do not.

```c
_Atomic(const int) counter;
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
const _Atomic(int) counter;
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

Write the other qualifiers outside the specifier.
For an array, make its elements atomic instead of the array.

### E2956: atomic-member-access

The program accesses a member of an atomic structure or union.
C11 6.5.2.3p5 makes that access undefined behavior.

The access is an error where it is evaluated; `sizeof` of the member is allowed.
Atomic operations act on the complete object, not on one member.

```c
struct pair { int a, b; };
_Atomic struct pair whole;
int main(void) { return whole.a; }
```

```c
struct pair { _Atomic int a, b; };
struct pair whole;
int main(void) { return whole.a; }
```

Make each member an atomic object when the members change one at a time.

### E2957: always-inline-returns-twice

An `always_inline` function makes a call that returns twice.
Inlining would move the second return of the call into the caller.
An ordinary call would return from a frame that no longer exists when the
jump comes. GCC 14 refuses such a function too.

```c
int setjmp(void *);
static char point[512];
static inline __attribute__((always_inline)) int mark(void) { return setjmp(point); }
int main(void) { return mark(); }
```

Fix: none

Remove `always_inline` and call `setjmp` in the function that later jumps
back to it.

### E2958: unsupported-enumeration-underlying-type

EvoCC does not implement this fixed underlying type of an enumeration.
GCC 14 converts to an enumeration whose underlying type is `_Bool` as to `_Bool`, and Apple clang truncates.
EvoCC therefore refuses `_Bool` there, and also `__int128`, an atomic type and an aligned typedef.
Use another integer type, such as `unsigned char`.

```c
enum flag : _Bool { no, yes };
int main(void) { return no; }
```

```c
enum flag : unsigned char { no, yes };
int main(void) { return no; }
```

### E2959: unsupported-complex-type-generic-call

A type-generic call selects a complex function, or has a complex argument, of a type whose values EvoCC does not run.
These types are GCC's `_Float16 _Complex` and the other `_FloatN _Complex` and `_FloatNx _Complex` types.
`__builtin_tgmath`, which glibc's `<tgmath.h>` uses, selects a complex function for a complex argument.
Use a `float`, `double` or `long double` complex argument.

```c
double real(double);
float realf(float);
_Float32 _Complex value;
int main(void) { return (int)__builtin_tgmath(realf, real, value); }
```

```c
static double twice(double value) { return 2 * value; }
static float twicef(float value) { return 2 * value; }
static double _Complex ctwice(double _Complex value) { return 2 * value; }
static float _Complex ctwicef(float _Complex value) { return 2 * value; }
int main(void) {
    double _Complex value = __builtin_tgmath(twicef, twice, ctwicef, ctwice, 1.0 + 2.0i);
    return __real__ value == 2.0 && __imag__ value == 4.0 ? 0 : 1;
}
```

### E2960: unmodeled-complex-constant

A constant product or quotient of floating complex values needs a model of the target's complex helpers, and EvoCC has none for this target.
On Darwin, compiler-rt computes complex multiplication and division.
EvoCC has no model of those helpers, so it cannot give the value during translation.

Flags: --target=aarch64-apple-darwin

```c
static const double _Complex product = (1.0 + 2.0i) * (3.0 + 4.0i);
int main(void) { return product == -5.0 + 10.0i ? 0 : 1; }
```

```c
static const double _Complex product = -5.0 + 10.0i;
int main(void) { return product == -5.0 + 10.0i ? 0 : 1; }
```

Write the value of the product or quotient, or compute it at run time.

### E2961: mixed-half-formats

An operator has a `_Float16` operand and a `__bf16` operand.
The two half formats have no common real type, because neither value set contains the other.

Binary16 has more significand bits, and bfloat16 has a larger exponent range.
C23 H.4.2 leaves such a mixture undefined, and the reference compilers do not agree on it.
Convert one operand to the format of the other, or convert both operands to `float`.

```c
int main(void) {
    _Float16 a = 1;
    __bf16 b = 2;
    return a + b > 2;
}
```

```c
int main(void) {
    _Float16 a = 1;
    __bf16 b = 2;
    return (float)a + (float)b > 2;
}
```

## E3xxx

### E3001: read-of-uninitialized-object

The executed path reads object bytes that have not been initialized.
A declaration without an initializer does not give an automatic scalar a value.

EvoCC tracks initialized bytes instead of substituting zero for missing data.
Initialize the object on every path before reading it.

```c
int main(void) { int value; return value; }
```

```c
int main(void) { int value = 0; return value; }
```

### E3002: integer-division-by-zero

The executed integer division has a zero divisor.
The numerator does not make this operation valid, even when it is zero.

C does not define integer division by zero.
Check the divisor and choose the required error behavior before dividing.

```c
int main(void) { int divisor = 0; return 1 / divisor; }
```

```c
int main(void) {
    int divisor = 0;
    if (divisor == 0) return 0;
    return 1 / divisor;
}
```

### E3003: integer-remainder-by-zero

The executed remainder operation has a zero divisor.
There is no valid integer remainder for this operation.

C does not define a remainder operation with a zero divisor.
Handle zero separately before evaluating `%`.

```c
int main(void) { int divisor = 0; return 1 % divisor; }
```

```c
int main(void) {
    int divisor = 0;
    return divisor == 0 ? 0 : 1 % divisor;
}
```

### E3004: signed-integer-overflow

An executed signed integer operation has a result outside its permitted range.
Negating the minimum value and dividing it by minus one can also cause overflow.

The checked profile reports overflow instead of assuming signed arithmetic wraps.
Check the range before the operation, or use a suitable wider arithmetic type.

```c
int main(void) { int value = 2147483647; return value + 1; }
```

```c
int main(void) {
    int value = 2147483647;
    long result = (long)value + 1;
    return result != 2147483648L;
}
```

The conversion must occur before addition, not after an overflowing result.

### E3005: invalid-shift-count

The shift count is negative or at least the width of the promoted left operand.
The width of the result variable does not change that operand's shift width.

C restricts the count for both left and right shifts.
Check the count before shifting instead of relying on hardware count masking.

```c
int main(void) { int count = 32; return 1U << count; }
```

```c
int main(void) {
    int count = 32;
    if (count < 0 || count >= 32) return 0;
    return (1U << count) != 0;
}
```

### E3006: invalid-signed-left-shift

This code names an explicit IR obligation for a signed left shift.
The current GNU source profile does not insert that obligation.

For a valid count, this profile defines the result as the low bits of the product.
It still checks the count and reports E3005 when the count is invalid.

Trigger: none
Reason: C lowering does not assert signed_shl_defined in the current GNU profile.

The code remains readable for explicit IR obligations.
Do not treat a negative left operand alone as an E3006 source trigger.

### E3007: scalar-function-fell-off-end

This withdrawn diagnostic identified a reached end of a non-void function.
The current IR contract represents that missing result as poison instead.

A missing return does not supply a defined scalar value to the caller.
Write an explicit return on each path that needs a result.

Trigger: none
Reason: the authority table withdraws this code in favor of the poison-result contract.

```c
int value(void) { return 0; }
int main(void) { return value(); }
```

### E3008: interpreter-fuel-exhausted

The interpreter reached its execution step limit.
This is a resource limit, not proof that the program has undefined behavior.

EvoCC bounds interpreted execution so a check cannot run without limit.
Inspect long-running loops and use a finite workload when testing termination.

```c
int main(void) { for (;;) {} }
```

```c
int main(void) {
    unsigned count = 0;
    while (count < 10) ++count;
    return count != 10;
}
```

For an intentional long-running service, a step limit does not identify a source defect.

### E3009: null-pointer-access

The executed memory access uses a null pointer.
A null pointer does not identify storage for the requested object.

C does not permit reading or writing an object through a null pointer.
Provide a live object or handle the null case before accessing memory.

```c
int main(void) { int *p = 0; return *p; }
```

```c
int main(void) { int value = 0; int *p = &value; return *p; }
```

### E3010: dangling-pointer-access

The pointer refers to an object whose lifetime has ended.
Keeping the address does not keep the object alive.

An access requires live storage, not just an address that was once valid.
Keep the object alive until its last use or copy its value before leaving its scope.

```c
int main(void) {
    int *p;
    { int value = 0; p = &value; }
    return *p;
}
```

```c
int main(void) {
    int result;
    { int value = 0; result = value; }
    return result;
}
```

### E3011: out-of-bounds-memory-access

The executed access extends outside the object's permitted storage.
A one-past pointer can describe an endpoint but cannot be dereferenced.

C accesses must stay within the applicable object bounds.
Check indices and access sizes before reading or writing.

```c
int main(void) { int values[2] = {0}; return values[2]; }
```

```c
int main(void) { int values[2] = {0}; return values[1]; }
```

### E3012: misaligned-memory-access

The pointer is not aligned for the executed access.
A cast changes the pointer type but does not align the address.

C typed accesses must meet the required alignment.
Use aligned storage or copy bytes into an aligned object before a typed read.

```c
int main(void) {
    int values[2] = {0};
    char *p = (char *)values;
    return *(int *)(p + 1);
}
```

```c
int main(void) { int values[2] = {0}; return values[1]; }
```

### E3013: invalid-pointer-representation

The interpreter cannot resolve the pointer representation to a permitted target.
An arbitrary integer address is not evidence of a live object.

EvoCC's memory model keeps pointer identity and exposed-address information.
Use a pointer derived from a live object instead of inventing an address.

```c
int main(void) { return *(int *)1; }
```

```c
int main(void) { int value = 0; return *(&value); }
```

This interpreter result does not model access to a platform-specific hardware address.

### E3014: write-to-read-only-object

The executed store writes an object marked read-only.
A pointer cast does not change that object's storage permission.

C does not permit modifying a string literal or a const-defined object this way.
Use a writable copy when the program needs to change the data.

```c
int main(void) { char *text = "abc"; text[0] = 0; return 0; }
```

```c
int main(void) { char text[] = "abc"; text[0] = 0; return text[0]; }
```

### E3015: call-through-null-function-pointer

The executed indirect call uses a null function pointer.
No function is selected by that value.

C requires a valid function target when a call is executed.
Initialize the callback or handle a missing callback before calling it.

```c
int main(void) { int (*callback)(void) = 0; return callback(); }
```

```c
int result(void) { return 0; }
int main(void) { int (*callback)(void) = result; return callback(); }
```

### E3016: call-through-non-function-pointer

The indirect call's pointer identifies data rather than a function.
Changing the pointer's type does not turn object storage into executable code.

The interpreter distinguishes object addresses from function identities.
Pass a real function pointer with the required signature.

```c
int main(void) {
    int object = 0;
    int (*callback)(void) = (int (*)(void))&object;
    return callback();
}
```

```c
int result(void) { return 0; }
int main(void) { int (*callback)(void) = result; return callback(); }
```

### E3017: indirect-call-signature-mismatch

An IR indirect call disagrees with the function-pointer type at the call site.
This is a malformed call interface, not a runtime selection of the wrong function.

The validator checks the call arguments and results against that pointer type.
Fix the IR producer so the instruction uses the declared interface.

Trigger: none
Reason: this validator diagnostic needs malformed IR, not a well-formed C call.

For a C cast that selects an incompatible function at runtime, see E3019.

### E3018: invalid-lifetime-end

The contract assigns this code to an invalid explicit end of an object's lifetime.
The object must be automatic storage owned by the current frame at its base address.

An IR lifetime operation must not destroy a foreign frame or static object.
Correct the producer of the lifetime operation rather than suppressing the check.

Trigger: none
Reason: C has no explicit lifetime.end operation, and the memory diagnostic currently uses E3007.

That code mapping differs from the authority table and needs a separate correction.
An ordinary use after scope exit instead reports E3010.

### E3019: function-pointer-target-signature-mismatch

The executed function pointer selects a function with an incompatible signature.
The pointer's declared call interface does not match that function's actual interface.

C does not permit calling a function through an incompatible function type.
Keep the pointer type consistent with the function definition.

```c
long result(long value) { return value; }
int main(void) {
    int (*callback)(int) = (int (*)(int))result;
    return callback(0);
}
```

```c
long result(long value) { return value; }
int main(void) { long (*callback)(long) = result; return callback(0); }
```

### E3020: not-lowered: checked-arithmetic

This withdrawn code identified a missing checked-arithmetic lowering path.
It must not be reused for a different diagnostic.

Current lowering represents supported arithmetic with explicit definedness obligations.
An executed signed overflow reports E3004 rather than this former limitation.

Trigger: none
Reason: the diagnostic authority table marks this lowering refusal as withdrawn.

```c
int main(void) { int value = 1; return value + 1 != 2; }
```

### E3021: not-lowered: asm

The selected execution or lowering path cannot handle this assembly statement.
Native support for an assembly form does not imply interpreter support.

Assembly can change machine state outside the interpreter's supported semantics.
EvoCC refuses the operation instead of assuming it has no effect.

```c
int main(void) { asm("nop"); return 0; }
```

```c
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

The fixed example removes a statement unnecessary for its result.
Do not remove assembly that performs required hardware or synchronization work.

### E3022: bit-builtin-zero-operand

A count-leading-zeros or count-trailing-zeros builtin received zero.
These builtin forms do not define a result for that input.

EvoCC checks the builtin's source contract rather than a hardware instruction's behavior.
Handle zero before calling the builtin.

```c
int main(void) { return __builtin_clz(0); }
```

```c
int main(void) {
    unsigned value = 0;
    int leading = value == 0 ? 32 : __builtin_clz(value);
    return leading != 32;
}
```

### E3023: not-lowered: bit-builtin

This withdrawn code identified missing lowering for bit builtins.
Current supported bit builtins do not use this refusal.

The implementation now lowers those operations with their operand requirements.
For a zero operand to a restricted count builtin, handle the input or expect E3022.

Trigger: none
Reason: the diagnostic authority table marks this lowering refusal as withdrawn.

```c
int main(void) { return __builtin_popcount(3U) != 2; }
```

### E3024: unreachable-reached

Execution reached `__builtin_unreachable()`.
The program's assertion that this path cannot execute was false.

This builtin is not a runtime check with a recovery path.
Handle the reachable case explicitly instead of declaring it impossible.

```c
int main(void) { __builtin_unreachable(); }
```

```c
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

### E3025: not-lowered: return-address

The contract reserves this code for unsupported return-address lowering.
It describes a target capability limit rather than an ordinary integer result.

An ancestor's return address depends on machine frames and calling conventions.
EvoCC must not invent that address when the requested level is unsupported.

Trigger: none
Reason: depth zero has activation-address lowering, admitted nonzero depths yield null, and out-of-range depths are E2913.

Pass the required caller information explicitly instead of inspecting its return address.

### E3026: not-lowered: static-relocation

A static initializer requires a relocation expression that lowering cannot represent.
Intermediate casts can make a label difference more than a plain address subtraction.

A relocation must preserve all source conversions, including narrowing.
EvoCC refuses an unsupported form instead of dropping a cast.

```c
int main(void) {
    static long offset = (signed char)(&&end - &&start);
start:
    if (offset) goto end;
    return 0;
end:
    return 1;
}
```

Fix: none

Choose an encoding that the target relocation format can represent.
Removing the narrowing cast changes the value and is not a general fix.

### E3027: overlapping-copy

A copy operation requires disjoint source and destination ranges, but they overlap.
Different starting addresses do not prove that the complete ranges are disjoint.

The `memcpy` contract does not permit overlapping ranges.
Use `memmove` when overlap is part of the intended operation.

```c
int main(void) { char data[4] = {0}; __builtin_memcpy(data + 1, data, 3); return 0; }
```

```c
int main(void) { char data[4] = {0}; __builtin_memmove(data + 1, data, 3); return 0; }
```

### E3029: not-lowered: computed-goto

This former refusal applied to computed-goto lowering.
It is withdrawn for the supported `br.indirect` representation.

A computed goto must still identify a valid destination in its function.
An invalid executed target is a different finding, E3048.

Trigger: none
Reason: supported C computed gotos now use br.indirect rather than this refusal.

```c
int main(void) { void *target = &&done; goto *target; done: return 0; }
```

### E3030: not-lowered: varargs

A variadic operation requires a type or ABI form outside the supported path.
This does not mean that all variadic calls are unsupported.

Each anonymous argument must be passed and retrieved using its real ABI classification.
EvoCC refuses unsupported forms instead of assigning them an unrelated scalar layout.

```c
struct S { _Float32 value; int tag; };
int take(int n, ...) {
    __builtin_va_list ap;
    __builtin_va_start(ap, n);
    struct S value = __builtin_va_arg(ap, struct S);
    return 0;
}
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

Fix: none

Use an implemented interface that preserves the required data and calling contract.
Replacing the argument type with `double` does not preserve this interface.

### E3031: not-lowered: frame-address

The requested low-level frame address is not available on the selected path.
The EvoIR interpreter rejects a nonzero `frame_address` depth when it executes it.

Frame layout is target-specific and cannot be guessed from source call structure.
Pass required data explicitly instead of depending on an ancestor's frame address.

Trigger: none
Reason: C activation-address builtins return null for admitted nonzero depths; this code remains for independently supplied EvoIR and invalid C-HIR.

```c
int read_value(const int *p) { return *p; }
int main(void) { int value = 0; return read_value(&value); }
```

### E3032: not-lowered: pointer-difference

This withdrawn code identified missing pointer-difference lowering.
Current pointer subtraction has an implemented path.

The implementation must still respect object identity and element size.
Subtract pointers only when the operation meets its object and range requirements.

Trigger: none
Reason: the diagnostic authority table marks this lowering refusal as withdrawn.

```c
int main(void) { int values[2]; return &values[1] - &values[0] != 1; }
```

### E3033: not-executed: wide-integer

An operation needs an integer width outside that operation's implemented path.
Support for a type does not imply support for every use of that type.

EvoCC keeps the full width instead of silently truncating to a host integer.
Use a supported operation or provide an explicit implementation for the required width.

```c
int main(void) { asm("" : : "i"((__int128)1 << 100)); return 0; }
```

Fix: none

This example cannot encode a 128-bit immediate through the supported assembly operand path.
Narrowing it to 64 bits would lose the bit it needs.

### E3034: not-lowered: function-pointer-arithmetic

This withdrawn code identified a former function-pointer arithmetic refusal.
The GNU target profile now uses exposed addresses for the supported operations.

This extension is not a portable ISO C function-pointer arithmetic guarantee.
Prefer an actual function pointer when selecting a function to call.

Trigger: none
Reason: the authority table withdraws this refusal in favor of exposed-address lowering.

```c
int result(void) { return 0; }
int main(void) { int (*p)(void) = result; return p(); }
```

### E3035: not-lowered: global-register-variable

This withdrawn code identified missing support for global register variables.
Current lowering represents their access through implicit assembly.

Binding an object to a machine register requires target-specific behavior.
Native lowering support does not make that register available to an interpreter.

Trigger: none
Reason: the authority table withdraws this code; global register access uses implicit asm.

Use ordinary C storage when no specific machine register is required.

### E3036: not-lowered: pointer-integer-conversion

This code is withdrawn and is never reported by the current contract.
It formerly named a pointer-to-integer or integer-to-pointer lowering limitation.

The supported conversion path retains the target's exposed-address rules.
A converted integer still needs a valid object or function target before access.

Trigger: none
Reason: the diagnostic authority table explicitly marks this code withdrawn and never reported.

An invalid pointer used for access can report E3013 instead.

### E3037: va-start-outside-variadic-signature

An IR `va_start` operation appears in a function with a nonvariadic signature.
That signature does not provide the anonymous arguments required by the operation.

The validator independently checks the IR function interface.
Fix the producer so it emits this operation only in a variadic function.

Trigger: none
Reason: the C front end rejects this source misuse with E2926 before IR validation.

E3037 remains a check on malformed IR and is distinct from a runtime argument mismatch.

### E3038: va-arg-mismatch

The variadic cursor cannot supply an argument of the requested type.
It can also have reached the end of the supplied arguments.

C requires each variadic read to agree with the corresponding promoted argument.
Keep the caller's types, the argument count, and the callee's reads consistent.

```c
int first(int n, ...) {
    __builtin_va_list ap;
    __builtin_va_start(ap, n);
    return __builtin_va_arg(ap, long);
}
int main(void) { return first(1, 0); }
```

```c
int first(int n, ...) {
    __builtin_va_list ap;
    __builtin_va_start(ap, n);
    int result = __builtin_va_arg(ap, int);
    __builtin_va_end(ap);
    return result;
}
int main(void) { return first(1, 0); }
```

### E3039: external-call-not-executable

Execution reached an external call that the interpreter cannot resolve.
A declaration supplies a type, not an executable function body.

The interpreter does not call arbitrary host libraries with target arguments.
Supply a supported definition or use native compilation with the required library.

```c
extern int result(void);
int main(void) { return result(); }
```

```c
int result(void) { return 0; }
int main(void) { return result(); }
```

### E3040: external-object-not-executable

Execution needs an external object whose storage is not available to the interpreter.
An `extern` declaration alone does not allocate that object.

A native linker can resolve another translation unit, but this execution lacks its storage.
Provide the object's definition or test the linked native program instead.

```c
extern int value;
int main(void) { return value; }
```

```c
int value = 0;
int main(void) { return value; }
```

### E3041: symbol-declared-and-defined

The module gives one symbol incompatible roles, such as an alias and a separate definition.
An ordinary compatible `extern` declaration followed by a definition is not this error.

Symbol resolution must select one coherent implementation or storage object.
Keep either the alias role or the separate definition, according to the intended linkage.

```c
int value = 0;
extern int other __attribute__((alias("value")));
int other = 0;
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
int value = 0;
extern int other __attribute__((alias("value")));
int main(void) { return other; }
```

### E3042: not-lowered: checked-arithmetic-width

This withdrawn code identified a checked-arithmetic width limitation.
It must not be reused for a new unsupported operation.

Current supported arithmetic paths retain their actual operand width and overflow checks.
A supported operation that overflows has a runtime diagnostic, not this old lowering refusal.

Trigger: none
Reason: the diagnostic authority table marks this lowering refusal as withdrawn.

```c
int main(void) { long value = 1; return value + 1 != 2; }
```

### E3043: not-lowered: object-function-pointer-conversion

This withdrawn code identified an object-pointer and function-pointer conversion limitation.
It does not describe a runtime call through an invalid function target.

A permitted conversion does not establish that the converted pointer can be called.
Use the correct pointer kind and preserve the identity of the actual target.

Trigger: none
Reason: the diagnostic authority table marks this lowering refusal as withdrawn.

A call through data storage reports E3016 on the executed path.

### E3045: not-lowered: ordered-pointer-comparison

This withdrawn code identified missing ordered pointer comparison lowering.
Supported pointer comparisons now have an implemented path.

An implemented comparison does not remove C's restrictions on comparable pointers.
Use pointers within the relationships permitted by the source and target profile.

Trigger: none
Reason: the diagnostic authority table marks this lowering refusal as withdrawn.

```c
int main(void) { int values[2]; return !(&values[0] < &values[1]); }
```

### E3047: builtin-trap-reached

Execution reached `__builtin_trap()`.
The program explicitly requested abnormal termination at this point.

The interpreter reports the trap instead of terminating its own host process.
Inspect the condition that selected this path before changing the trap.

```c
int main(void) { __builtin_trap(); }
```

```c
int main(void) { int valid = 1; if (!valid) __builtin_trap(); return 0; }
```

### E3048: invalid-indirect-branch-target

An executed computed goto does not identify a valid destination in its function.
Changing a label address numerically can destroy its target identity.

The interpreter checks the runtime address against the function's allowed destinations.
Keep an original label value instead of constructing an arbitrary branch address.

```c
int main(void) {
    void *target = &&done;
    unsigned long address = (unsigned long)target;
    target = (void *)(address + 1);
    goto *target;
done:
    return 0;
}
```

```c
int main(void) { void *target = &&done; goto *target; done: return 0; }
```

### E3049: not-lowered: floating-call-interface

A function interface uses a floating type outside the supported executable ABI.
Support for `float`, `double` and `long double` does not imply support for `_Float32` interfaces.

Arguments and results must keep their actual representation and calling convention.
EvoCC refuses an unsupported interface instead of substituting another type.
An HFA of `__bf16` members is refused too: GCC 14 passes it in general registers, and AAPCS64 uses vector registers.
On Darwin, a record that mixes `__bf16` and `_Float16` members is refused, because Apple clang passes it in vector registers.

```c
_Float32 identity(_Float32 value) { return value; }
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

Fix: none

Use a compiler that implements the required interface or redesign that interface explicitly.
Replacing it with a scalar would change the public ABI.

### E3050: not-lowered: floating-value

The expression needs a floating value operation outside the supported lowering path.
Arithmetic on vectors of `long double` lanes is one example of this boundary.
Vectors of `float` and `double` lanes execute lane by lane.

A known type layout does not establish executable arithmetic semantics.
EvoCC refuses the expression instead of computing only part of its value.

```c
typedef long double quad __attribute__((vector_size(32)));
int main(void) { quad a = {1.0L, 2.0L}; quad b = a + a; return b[1] != 4.0L; }
```

Fix: none

Use an implemented arithmetic contract that preserves each lane and its special values.
Discarding lanes is not a general fix.

### E3060: weak-internal-symbol

A symbol combines weak binding with internal linkage.
The resulting symbol contract is not valid for this module.

Weak binding participates in external symbol resolution.
Remove weak binding from a private definition, or deliberately give the symbol external linkage.

```c
static int value __attribute__((weak));
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
static int value;
int main(void) { return value; }
```

### E3061: alias-target-not-defined

A symbol alias does not resolve to a valid definition in this translation unit.
An external declaration alone does not define its target.

This alias form needs an actual target with a compatible symbol contract.
Define the target in the same translation unit and make the alias agree with it.

```c
extern int missing;
extern int other __attribute__((alias("missing")));
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
int value = 0;
extern int other __attribute__((alias("value")));
int main(void) { return other; }
```

### E3062: invalid-atomic-access

An IR or interpreter atomic access violates its type, width, alignment, or order contract.
This is distinct from a valid atomic operation applied to a null or dangling pointer.

Atomic accesses require specific access sizes and legal ordering combinations.
The validator and memory implementation check that contract before performing the operation.

Trigger: none
Reason: the C front end rejects unsupported atomic forms before this internal access check.

C operand and order errors report E2913 or E2947.
Ordinary pointer faults retain their memory diagnostic codes.

### E3066: object-size-check-failed

A checked C library call received a length larger than the size of its destination.
The C library stops the program at this call instead of writing past the object.

Fortified headers turn calls such as `memcpy` into `__builtin___memcpy_chk` with the destination size.
The check runs when a constant length does not prove that the destination is large enough.
Write no more bytes than the destination holds.

```c
static unsigned long length(void) { return 12; }
int main(void) {
    char buffer[8];
    __builtin___memset_chk(buffer, 0, length(), __builtin_object_size(buffer, 0));
    return buffer[0];
}
```

```c
int main(void) {
    char buffer[8];
    __builtin___memset_chk(buffer, 0, sizeof buffer, __builtin_object_size(buffer, 0));
    return buffer[0];
}
```

### E3067: not-executed: complex-arithmetic

The interpreter reached a floating complex product or quotient that it cannot compute for this target.
On Darwin, compiler-rt computes complex multiplication and division.
EvoCC has no model of those helpers, so neither interpreter executes the operation.
Native code calls the helpers, and the other complex operations run in the interpreters.

Flags: --target=aarch64-apple-darwin

```c
int main(void) {
    volatile double _Complex a = 1.0 + 2.0i;
    double _Complex product = a * a;
    return __real__ product == -3.0 ? 0 : 1;
}
```

```c
int main(void) {
    volatile double _Complex a = 1.0 + 2.0i;
    double _Complex sum = a + a;
    return __real__ sum == 2.0 ? 0 : 1;
}
```

Check the product or quotient with the Linux target, or run the native program.

### E3101: evoir-lowering-failed

Lowering could not construct valid EvoIR for this source.
The detail after the header identifies the failed operation or validation rule.

EvoCC checks generated IR instead of executing an inconsistent module.
Reduce unexpected failures to a small source example and report them with the full diagnostic.

```c
int main(void) { goto *(void *)1; }
```

```c
int main(void) { void *target = &&done; goto *target; done: return 0; }
```

This example has no valid label target; the fix supplies one.
Other lowering failures can be compiler defects rather than source errors.

## W0xxx

### W0001: unused variable

A variable with no external linkage is declared but never referenced.
The declaration can hide a missing operation or old code.

C permits unused variables.
EvoCC reports this warning only when it is enabled.

Flags: -Werror=unused-variable

```c
int main(void) { int count = 3; return 0; }
```

```c
int main(void) { int count = 3; return count; }
```

### W0002: unused parameter

A function parameter is never referenced in its definition.
Its caller still passes the argument.

C permits unused parameters and unnamed prototype parameters.
EvoCC checks definitions, not prototypes, when this warning is enabled.

Flags: -Werror=unused-parameter

```c
int value(int count) { return 0; }
int main(void) { return value(3); }
```

```c
int value(int count) { return count; }
int main(void) { return value(3); }
```

### W0003: function has no declaration

A call names a function with no visible declaration.
The compiler cannot check its intended interface.

C99 and later require a declaration before the call.
EvoCC denies this by default in these modes and warns in C89 modes.

Flags: -Werror=implicit-function-declaration

```c
int main(void) { return value(); }
```

```c
int value(void) { return 3; }
int main(void) { return value(); }
```

### W0004: declaration has no type specifier

A declaration omits its type specifier.
The legacy interpretation supplies int, which might not be the intended type.

C89 permitted implicit int in these declarations.
Later C modes require an explicit type, and EvoCC reports the omission.

Flags: -Werror=implicit-int

```c
main(void) { return 0; }
```

```c
int main(void) { return 0; }
```

### W0005: function does not return the required value

A non-void function can reach its end without a return value.
A caller can receive an undefined result if it uses the missing value.

C requires a value when the caller uses a non-void result.
Reaching the end of main is a special case that returns zero.

Flags: -Werror=return-type

```c
int value(int x) { if (x) return 3; }
int main(void) { return value(0); }
```

```c
int value(int x) { if (x) return 3; return 0; }
int main(void) { return value(0); }
```
